summary: Summarizes requirements for resource priority mechanisms in SIP, meaning ways of prioritizing access to circuit-switched networks, end systems and proxy resources for emergency preparedness communications. It is informational.

eli5.summary: During an emergency, important calls should go first. This note lists what SIP would need in order to give some calls priority.

questions: what are sip resource priority requirements
how can sip prioritize emergency calls
what is an ets call in sip
what security requirements apply to sip priority
subtitle: What SIP would need so that emergency preparedness calls can get through when networks are congested.

tldr.problem: During disasters, telephone circuits, IP bandwidth and gateways between the two networks can become congested, which makes it hard for emergency workers to coordinate.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists five resources that may need prioritized access, four network combinations, and 17 general requirements plus 12 security requirements for a SIP priority indication.
tldr.outcome: It specifies no protocol. It is a requirements document that later protocol work could be measured against.

today: RFC 3487 is an Informational RFC and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a requirements statement for SIP resource priority, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Why Prioritize Access
sections.content:
In an emergency, communications resources such as telephone circuits, IP bandwidth and gateways between circuit-switched and IP networks may become congested. Heavy usage, loss of resources in a disaster, and attacks can all cause it. That makes it hard for people charged with emergency assistance, recovery or law enforcement to coordinate.

This memo covers real-time applications that use the Session Initiation Protocol (RFC 3261), including voice over IP, multimedia conferencing and instant messaging and presence. It takes no position on which mode of communication is best during an emergency. The act of giving some requests preferred access is called resource prioritization.

The document describes requirements, not protocol features. It says that a mechanism does not have to be a SIP header field, method or URI parameter.
sections.eli5: When too many people call at once, the lines jam. This note asks how helpers could be let through first, and it only lists what is needed, not how to build it.

sections.title: The Five Resources
sections.content:
The memo names five kinds of resource that might need prioritized access:

  • Gateway resources: the finite number of channels (trunks) on a gateway to a circuit-switched network (CSN). Access could be given by priority queuing or preemption.
  • CSN resources: circuits away from the gateway, handled by traditional mechanisms such as MLPP and GETS. Specifying CSN behavior is out of scope, but a central requirement is that an IP endpoint can invoke them.
  • IP network resources: bandwidth for audio and video. This is called orthogonal to SIP and is left to another document.
  • Receiving end system resources: for example automatic call distribution systems and media servers, which can handle only a finite number of sessions. A prioritized call may need to preempt an existing call.
  • SIP proxy resources: proxy capacity. Dropping or queuing requests under overload is called an implementation issue outside the protocol requirements.

Responses should get the same treatment as the matching request. There is no requirement that one mechanism serve all five resources.
sections.eli5: Think of five bottlenecks, like the doors at a busy stadium. The note names each door where helpers might need to go first.

sections.title: Network Topologies and Models
sections.content:
Four combinations of IP and circuit-switched networks are considered: IP end-to-end, IP-to-CSN, CSN-to-IP, and CSN-IP-CSN (IP bridging). In the bridging case the two CSN sides may use different signaling protocols, so simply wrapping the original CSN information is not enough. A CSN-to-IP gateway is unlikely to know whether the final destination is in the IP network, the CSN or, through SIP forking, both.

Four IP network models also matter, each inheriting the restrictions of the one before: pre-configured for ETS, transparent, SIP/RTP transparent and restricted SIP networks. The memo says it is preferable that protocol enhancements work at least in SIP/RTP transparent networks and are added explicitly to restricted SIP networks.

Emergency calls by the public (such as 911 and 112) are a different topic. The call identifier already marks them, so they do not need a resource priority indication.
sections.eli5: Calls can travel over old phone lines, over the internet, or both. Some networks let anything through and some are strict, so the plan has to work in as many of them as possible.

sections.title: The General Requirements
sections.content:
Section 9 sets out 17 requirements, REQ-1 to REQ-17, for what it calls a SIP indication: a marker that makes a request a labelled request. The memo warns that not all of them can be met at once. Some are tradeoffs.

  • Not specific to one scheme or country, and independent of network architecture (REQ-1, REQ-2).
  • Invisible to the IP layer, so it must be a valid SIP request and out-of-band signaling is not acceptable (REQ-3).
  • Existing circuit-switched schemes must map to SIP, without loss of information when both CSNs use the same scheme (REQ-4, REQ-5).
  • Extensible naming (REQ-6), and separation of policy and mechanism: the indication invokes a named policy rather than spelling out the treatment (REQ-7).
  • Works for any SIP method and any address (REQ-8, REQ-10).
  • A default that treats the call no worse than an unmarked call (REQ-9).
  • Priority is not decided by user identity or network location alone (REQ-11, REQ-12).
  • Support for several schemes at once and discovery of supported ones (REQ-13, REQ-14).
  • Testable outside emergencies, works with third-party call control, and visible to proxies (REQ-15, REQ-16, REQ-17).
sections.eli5: The rules say the priority sticker must work everywhere, must not need special roads, must be testable on a normal day, and must never make a call worse off than before.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The memo says any resource priority mechanism can be abused to obtain resources and deny service to other users. So a request carrying a priority indication needs more rigorous authentication than a regular one. The twelve security requirements, SEC-1 to SEC-12, cover four areas.

  • Authentication and authorization (SEC-1 to SEC-7): stronger than for public emergency calls, able to survive attack, independent of the mechanism used, usable on devices the user does not own, and resistant to replay, cut-and-paste and bid-down attacks. Authentication has to happen on the IP side, not by using a scarce CSN circuit.
  • Confidentiality and integrity (SEC-8): header fields such as To, From and Via are sensitive. Unauthorized users must not be able to tell that a request uses priority.
  • Anonymity (SEC-9): callers may stay anonymous toward the destination while still authenticating to the network.
  • Denial of service (SEC-10 to SEC-12): minimize what unauthorized users can consume, and do not amplify attacks by sending more than one packet or SIP request to an unverified address.
sections.eli5: A priority pass is only useful if it cannot be faked or stolen. So the note asks for strong proof of who you are, secrecy about who is calling whom, and protection against floods of fake calls.

items.title: Gateway
items.text: Finite trunks between IP and the circuit-switched network.

items.title: CSN
items.text: Circuits inside the telephone network, handled by MLPP and GETS.

items.title: IP network
items.text: Bandwidth for audio and video; left to another document.

items.title: Receiving end system
items.text: Finite sessions on call distribution systems and media servers.

items.title: SIP proxy
items.text: Request handling capacity; an implementation issue.
